concepts.label: Variables and assignment
concepts.summary: A name bound to a value. The right-hand side is evaluated first, then the name is bound to the result, which is why count = count + 1 is an instruction rather than a contradiction.

source_spans.quote: A variable is a name bound to a value.
rebinding one does not disturb anything else

misconceptions.statement: The single equals sign states that the two sides are equal, so count = count + 1 is impossible.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Every prior year of mathematics teaches that = is a claim about two equal quantities, and x = x + 1 has no solutions there.
misconceptions.correction: In Python = is an instruction: evaluate the right side, then bind the name to the result. The claim about equality is the double equals sign, ==.

misconceptions.statement: After b = a, changing a also changes b, because the two names are tied together.
misconceptions.why_plausible: The line reads like it sets up a relationship, and spreadsheet formulas really do keep following the cell they refer to.
misconceptions.correction: Assignment happens once. b = a copies the reference at that moment; rebinding a afterwards leaves b holding the old value.

concepts.label: Types and conversion
concepts.summary: Every value has a type, and the type decides what an operator means. Plus adds two numbers and joins two strings, so mixing them is an error rather than a guess.

source_spans.quote: the same operator can mean different things depending on the types it is given

misconceptions.statement: "5" and 5 are the same value written two ways, so "5" + 5 gives 10.
misconceptions.why_plausible: They look identical on screen and read aloud the same, and some other languages do convert silently between them.
misconceptions.correction: They are different types. Python refuses to guess whether plus should add or join, and raises a TypeError. Convert first with int("5").

misconceptions.statement: If the user types digits, what you get back is a number you can do arithmetic with.
misconceptions.why_plausible: The user really did type a number, and nothing on screen distinguishes the digits they typed from an integer.
misconceptions.correction: input always hands back a string, whatever was typed. Wrap it in int() or float() when you want to calculate with it.

concepts.label: Printing versus returning
concepts.summary: print displays a value to a person as a side effect and hands back None. Showing a value and producing a value are different acts.

source_spans.quote: What print does not do is give the value back to your program.
A function that prints its answer instead of returning it is a function whose answer nobody else can use.

misconceptions.statement: result = print("hello") puts the string "hello" into result.
misconceptions.why_plausible: The word appears on screen the instant the line runs, so it plainly went somewhere, and the interactive prompt echoes values in exactly the same way.
misconceptions.correction: print writes to the screen and hands back None, so result is None. A value your program needs has to be returned, not printed.

concepts.label: Lists
concepts.summary: An ordered collection written in square brackets. Order is part of the value, len reports the count, and append adds to the end.

source_spans.quote: A list holds several values in order
Order is part of the list

misconceptions.statement: A list is just a bag of values, so [1, 2] and [2, 1] are the same list.
misconceptions.why_plausible: For many everyday purposes the order of a shopping list does not matter, and sets in mathematics genuinely ignore it.
misconceptions.correction: Order is part of a list's identity. [1, 2] and [2, 1] are different lists and compare as unequal.

concepts.label: Indexing from zero
concepts.summary: Items are reached by position in square brackets, counting from zero, so the last valid index of a list is one less than its length.

source_spans.quote: the last index is always one less than the length

misconceptions.statement: The first item of a list is scores[1], and a list of three items has a scores[3].
misconceptions.why_plausible: Counting anything else in life starts at one, and "the first item" and "item one" mean the same thing in English.
misconceptions.correction: The first item is scores[0] and the last of three is scores[2]. Asking for scores[3] raises an IndexError.

concepts.label: For loops and range
concepts.summary: A for loop rebinds a name to each item of a sequence in turn and runs the block once per item. range counts up to, but never reaches, the number given.

source_spans.quote: A for loop runs the same block of code once for each item in a sequence.
The range function stops before the number you give it

misconceptions.why_plausible: "Up to three" means up to and including three in ordinary English, and counting out loud starts at one.
misconceptions.correction: range(3) produces 0, 1 and 2 — three numbers, never 3. That is the same convention as indexing, which is why range(len(items)) is exactly the valid indexes.

misconceptions.statement: for score in scores binds score to each position, so you index with it.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Loops in some other languages really do hand you a counter, and the two forms look alike on the page.
misconceptions.correction: for score in scores binds score to each item itself. Use enumerate when you want the position as well.

misconceptions.statement: Removing items from a list while looping over it is fine, because the loop re-reads the list each time.
misconceptions.why_plausible: The loop clearly does look at the list on every pass, so it seems as though it would notice the change.
misconceptions.correction: The loop tracks its position by number. Removing an item shifts the rest down and the loop skips one. Build a new list instead.
